question: We're playing best of five games to 11. In the third game, when do we switch ends?

answer.reasoning: The question is about the Alternative Laws format best-of-5-games-11. The relevant source is alt-best-of-5-games-11:8.1.3, which replaces the standard third-game rule for that format; laws-8.1.3 gives the standard Laws rule for comparison. The sources do not give a mid-third-game change for best-of-5-games-11; they give an end-of-third-game change conditional on a fourth game, and separately a fifth-game change at 6 points.
answer.answer: Under the standard Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, players change ends "in the third game when a side first scores 11 points, except in Handicap Matches (BWF Statute Section 4.1.3)". For the Alternative Laws of Badminton 2.0 format best-of-5-games-11, in force 2027-01-04, the third-game rule is different: players change ends "at the end of the third game, if there is to be a fourth game;". So in best of five games to 11, you switch ends at the end of the third game only when a fourth game is going to be played; the sources do not state a mid-third-game change for this format.

question: My opponent shouted 'fault!' while I was playing my shot. What's the ruling?

answer.reasoning: The sources directly answer this: ITTO 5.9.1.4 says a player calling ‘fault’, etc. to the opponent when making a stroke or after the opponent has made a stroke is a deliberate distraction under Law 13.4.5, and Laws 13.4.5 makes deliberately distracting an opponent by shouting or gestures a fault. The question’s facts (opponent shouted ‘fault!’ while the user was playing a shot) match the ITTO condition. ITTO 5.9.1.3 is about shouting to a partner, so it does not apply here.
answer.answer: It is a fault by your opponent. Under the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, a player calling ‘fault’, etc. to the opponent when making a stroke or after the opponent has made a stroke “shall be considered a deliberate distraction (Law 13.4.5)”. Under the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Law 13.4.5 makes it a fault if, in play, a player “deliberately distracts an opponent by any action such as shouting or making gestures”. Because the shout was directed at you while you were playing your shot, the ruling is a fault against the opponent under Law 13.4.5.

question: When do we replay a rally? List every situation that counts as a let.

answer.reasoning: The question asks two things: when a rally is replayed, and every situation that counts as a let. Law 14.3 answers the replay question directly. Law 14.2 and its sub-clauses 14.2.1–14.2.7 (with 14.2.3 expanded into 14.2.3.1 and 14.2.3.2, which I read because 14.2.3 ends with a colon) give the complete list of let situations. Law 14.1 says who calls the let, and ITTO 5.9.1.2 adds the umpire guidance that a shuttle from an adjacent court is not automatically a let. Together these sources fully answer the question.
answer.answer: A rally is replayed when a 'let' is called: play since the last service does not count, and the player who served last serves again (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Law 14.3). 'Let' is called by the umpire, or by a player if there is no umpire, to halt play (Law 14.1). Under Law 14.2 of the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, it shall be a 'let' if: (1) the server serves before the receiver is ready (Law 9.4) [14.2.1]; (2) during service, the receiver and the server are both faulted [14.2.2]; (3) after the service is returned, the shuttle is caught on the net and remains suspended on its top [14.2.3.1], or, after passing over the net, is caught in the net [14.2.3.2]; (4) during play, the shuttle disintegrates and the base completely separates from the rest of the shuttle [14.2.4]; (5) in the opinion of the umpire, play is disrupted or a player of the opposing side is distracted by a coach [14.2.5]; (6) a line judge is unsighted and the umpire or Instant Review System is unable to make a decision [14.2.6]; or (7) any unforeseen or accidental situation has occurred [14.2.7]. Additionally, per Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 5.9.1.2, a shuttle coming onto the court from an adjacent court is not automatically a let: a 'let' shall not be called in such circumstances if, in the opinion of the Umpire, the shuttle has not obstructed or distracted the players.

‘Let’ shall be called by the umpire, or by a player (if there is no umpire), to halt play.

the server serves before the receiver is ready (Law 9.4);

question: My partner cut his hand mid-game and it's bleeding. How long can we stop, and who can come on court to help?

answer.reasoning: The question asks two things: (1) how long play can stop for a bleeding hand injury mid-game, and (2) who may come on court to help. The sources answer both directly. For duration: itto-5.14.2 gives the specific rule for a blood-flowing injury (delay until bleeding stops, wound dressed, or Referee advises otherwise); itto-3.6.1.4 requires the Referee to resolve the situation 'well within a few minutes'; itto-5.14.1 and itto-3.6.1.2 prohibit treatment causing undue delay on court (quick relief such as a bandage is allowed, time-consuming treatment only in regular intervals); itto-5.14.1 says the Umpire times the delay; laws-16.3.1 covers suspension of play generally. For who may come on court: itto-3.6.1.1 (Referee and Tournament Doctor go on court immediately when called), itto-5.14.1 (Referee decides whether the Tournament Doctor or anyone else is required), itto-3.6.1.3 (maximum two persons on court to assist/advise/translate, with the same consideration for the opposing side), and itto-3.6.1.6 (severe-injury exception). Together these fully answer the question, so no refusal is needed.
answer.answer: How long you can stop: For a blood-flowing injury, the game is delayed until the bleeding stops, the wound is suitably dressed, or the Referee advises the Umpire otherwise [itto-5.14.2]. The Referee must resolve the injury situation as quickly as possible and 'well within a few minutes' so play can be resumed or abandoned, and may point to potential disqualification if the player is suspected of exploiting the injury to regain wind or repeatedly hesitates in deciding to continue or abandon [itto-3.6.1.4]. No treatment causing undue delay may be given on court — the Tournament Doctor may apply quick relief such as a bandage on a bleeding injury, but no time-consuming treatment is allowed except in the regular intervals, and only if it can be (nearly) completed before the interval ends [itto-5.14.1, itto-3.6.1.2]. The Umpire times the delay caused by the injury [itto-5.14.1]. More generally, the umpire may suspend play for such period as the umpire considers necessary when necessitated by circumstances not within the players' control [laws-16.3.1]. Who can come on court: when the Umpire calls, the Referee and the Tournament Doctor shall immediately go on court [itto-3.6.1.1]; the Referee decides whether the Tournament Doctor or anyone else is required on court [itto-5.14.1]; and the Referee may allow a maximum of two persons on court to assist and advise the injured player and help with translation — with the opposing side allowed the same consideration in fairness [itto-3.6.1.3]. Exception: in a severe injury where there is no doubt the player cannot continue, the regular process is disregarded and the Tournament Doctor provides first aid until the player can be transported to hospital [itto-3.6.1.6]. All rules cited are from Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, except the suspension-of-play rule, which is from Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26.

question: Water started dripping from the roof onto our court mid-game. What happens to the match and the score?

answer.reasoning: The question asks what happens to a match and its score when water makes the court unplayable mid-game. The given sources cover this directly: itto-5.11.3 (court temporarily not playable → suspend until suitable), itto-5.11.2 (suspension warranted by circumstances affecting playing conditions), itto-5.11.4 (umpire's call and notation on suspension), laws-16.3.3 (existing score stands on suspension), and itto-5.11.5 (procedure on resumption). A search confirmed laws-16.3.3 is the score rule and no additional clause is needed. Together these fully answer the question.
answer.answer: Water dripping onto the court makes it 'temporarily not playable', so the Umpire shall call the Referee (or the Referee shall go onto the court) and play is suspended until the court and its immediate surroundings are again suitable for play (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 5.11.3). More generally, play may be suspended by the Referee or Umpire when warranted by a circumstance affecting playing conditions (ITTO 7.0 (5), Clause 5.11.2). When play is suspended, the Umpire calls "Play is suspended" and notes "S" on the scoring device or score-sheet (ITTO 7.0 (5), Clause 5.11.4). The score is unaffected: under Law 16.3.3 of the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, "If play is suspended, the existing score shall stand and play shall be resumed from that point." When play resumes, the Umpire notes the duration of the suspension, ensures the players are on the correct side of the net and in the correct service courts, then calls "Are you ready?" followed by the score and "Play" (ITTO 7.0 (5), Clause 5.11.5).

citations.quote: If, during a match, a court or its immediate surroundings needs repair, or it is temporarily not playable, the Umpire shall call the Referee (or the Referee shall go onto the court) and play be suspended until the court and its immediate surroundings are again suitable for play.
Play may be suspended by the Referee or Umpire if warranted by a circumstance affecting playing conditions.
When play is suspended, the Umpire shall call: “Play is suspended” and note “S” on the scoring device or score-sheet, if used.
If play is suspended, the existing score shall stand and play shall be resumed from that point.

When play resumes after the suspension, the Umpire shall note the duration of the suspension and ensure that the players are on the correct side of the net and in the correct service courts, then call “Are you ready?” followed by the score and “Play”.

question: My opponent keeps flicking sweat onto the court. What can the umpire do about it?

answer.reasoning: The question is directly answered by itto-5.9.1.6, which covers a player throwing sweat or contaminating the court: the umpire reminds the player the conduct is unacceptable and applies Law 16.7 if necessary. Law 16.7.1 (read in full) lists how the umpire administers a breach — warning, fault if previously warned, or fault for flagrant offence — and 16.7.2 adds that on faulting a side the umpire reports immediately to the Referee, who may disqualify. Together these fully answer what the umpire can do.
answer.answer: Under Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5) (in force 2025-04-26), Clause 5.9.1.6, a player throwing sweat or otherwise contaminating the court and its immediate surroundings 'shall be reminded that such conduct is unacceptable, with Law 16.7 applied, if necessary.' Under Law 16.7.1 of the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2) (in force 2025-04-26), the umpire administers the breach by: issuing a warning to the offending side; or faulting the offending side if previously warned; or faulting the offending side in cases of flagrant offence or breach. Under Law 16.7.2, on faulting a side the umpire 'shall report the offending side immediately to the Referee, who shall have the power to disqualify the offending side from the match.' So the escalation is: reminder/warning first, then a fault if it continues, then immediate report to the Referee, who can disqualify the offending side.

question: The line judge couldn't see whether the shuttle landed in. What happens to the rally?

answer.reasoning: The question asks what happens to a rally when the line judge is unsighted. The sources answer this directly: itto-8.5 and itto-8.8 cover the line judge's unsighted signal; itto-2.5 and itto-5.8.3 (with 5.8.3.1/5.8.3.2) cover the Umpire taking over the decision; laws-14.2.6, itto-2.5, and itto-5.8.3.3 cover the let when no decision can be made; itto-5.8.3.3, itto-2.5, and itto-5.8.9/5.8.9.1 cover the IRS exception. Together they fully answer the question, so refused is false.
answer.answer: The line judge must signal immediately that they are unsighted: per Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5) (in force 2025-04-26), Clause 8.5, "If unsighted, inform the Umpire immediately by putting both hands up to cover the eyes," and Clause 8.8 lists UNSIGHTED among "The approved hand signals". The rally then does not stop on the line judge's account: per Clause 2.5, "When another official is unsighted, the Umpire shall make the decision," and per Clause 5.8.3, "Where there is no Line Judge or if a Line Judge is unsighted, the Umpire shall immediately call:" — "Out" when the shuttle lands outside the line (then the score or "Service over" and then the score) [itto-5.8.3.1], or the score or "Service over" and then the score when the shuttle lands "in" [itto-5.8.3.2]. So normally the Umpire makes the in/out call and the rally continues. Only if no decision can be made does the rally become a let (replayed): under Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2) (in force 2025-04-26), Law 14.2.6, it is a 'let' if "a line judge is unsighted and the umpire or Instant Review System is unable to make a decision"; per ITTO Clause 2.5, "When no decision can be made, a 'let' shall be called"; and per ITTO Clause 5.8.3.3, the Umpire calls ""Let" followed by the score when the Umpire is unsighted." Exception: if an Instant Review System is in operation, the Umpire calls "Unsighted" and requests a decision from the system by raising the left hand above the head [itto-5.8.3.3], and per Clause 2.5 "unless IRS is in use, in which case it will be used to decide on the line call"; if the IRS indicates "NO DECISION" and the original call was unsighted, the Umpire calls "Let" [itto-5.8.9, itto-5.8.9.1].

question: How much clear space do we need behind the back line and beside the court?

answer.reasoning: The question asks for a specific amount of clear space behind the back line and beside the court. question: Can my coach get up from his chair and stand at the side of the court during the match?

answer.reasoning: The question asks whether a coach may stand court-side during a match. The directly relevant source is ITTO 7.0 (5) Clause 5.12.2, which states coaches must remain seated and must not stand court-side during the match except during permitted intervals, and separately restricts moving to another court to when the shuttle is not in play. Law 16.2.1 and 16.2.2 define those permitted intervals. Together these answer the question: standing court-side during play is not allowed; only during the Law 16.2 intervals is it permitted.
answer.answer: No. Under Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 5.12.2, coaches must be seated in their designated seats and must not stand court-side during the match, except during the permitted intervals in Law 16.2. Those intervals are: not exceeding 60 seconds during each game when the leading score reaches 11 points (except Handicap matches), and not exceeding 120 seconds between games. Separately, if the coach wishes to move to another court, that must be done while the shuttle is not in play.

question: What weight range is allowed for a plastic shuttle, and since our hall gets really hot and stuffy in summer, can we use a special type made for hot weather?

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts. (1) Weight of a plastic (non-feathered) shuttle: laws-2.3.3 says a non-feathered shuttle's measurements and weight are as in Laws 2.2.2, 2.2.3 and 2.2.6, with a variation of up to 10 per cent acceptable; laws-2.2.6 gives the feathered shuttle weight as 4.74 to 5.50 grams, which 2.3.3 incorporates by reference. (2) Hot-weather special shuttle: laws-2.4 allows modifications to the specifications with the approval of the Member Association concerned where atmospheric conditions due to altitude or climate make the standard shuttle unsuitable. Both parts are answered by the given sources; no tool call is needed.
answer.answer: A plastic (non-feathered) shuttle must have the weight given in Law 2.2.6 — 4.74 to 5.50 grams — but because of the difference in specific gravity and other properties of synthetic materials compared with feathers, a variation of up to 10 per cent is acceptable (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Clauses 2.3.3 and 2.2.6). As for hot weather: yes, modifications to the specifications may be made, but only with the approval of the Member Association concerned, and only in places where atmospheric conditions due to either altitude or climate make the standard shuttle unsuitable — so a hot, stuffy hall would need to qualify on that basis and the modified shuttle would need that approval (Clause 2.4).

question: My opponent got a yellow card for swearing during the warm-up, before the umpire called 'Play'. Does it cost him a point now, and does the card go on his record after the tournament?

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts: (1) whether a yellow card issued during warm-up, before 'Play', costs a point now, and (2) whether the card goes on the player's record after the tournament. Source itto-5.17.10 directly addresses pre-'Play' misconduct on the Field of Play and states the effect of any card given: no effect on the score, but taken into account if further offences occur during the match, cross-referencing Law 16.7.1.2. itto-5.17.3 confirms the yellow card is the warning procedure, and laws-16.7.1.2 shows the consequence only arises if the side is 'previously warned' and offends again. So part (1) is fully answered: no point is lost now. Part (2) — whether the card remains on a record after the tournament — is not addressed by any of the given sources; they only speak to the card's effect within the match. I answer part (1) from the sources and state that the sources do not cover the post-tournament record question.
answer.answer: No, the yellow card does not cost him a point now. Misconduct before the match while on the Field of Play before "Play" is called is treated under the warning/fault/disqualification procedures, and any card given "shall have no effect on the score of the match" — it only matters if further offences occur during the match, in which case the side may be faulted because it was "previously warned" (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Law 16.7.1.2; Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 5.17.10). As for whether the card goes on his record after the tournament: the sources given do not say — they cover only the card's effect on the match score and on later offences during the same match, not any post-tournament record.
